name: gegl
why: A node-graph image processing framework behind GIMP, letting you wire pixel transforms together in unusual ways.

brief.what_it_is: GEGL (Generic Graphics Library) is a data flow based image processing framework. You chain together processing operations to describe an image processing pipeline. It provides operations for image loading and storing, color adjustments, GIMP's artistic filters, and more. It can be used on the command line with the same syntax used to build processing flows interactively in GIMP, via gegl-graph. The homepage does not say exactly what file or stream formats go in and out, so that is unconfirmed.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage presents GEGL as a framework that gives floating point processing and non-destructive image processing to GNU Image Manipulation Program and other projects (imgflo, GNOME Photos, iconographer, and others).
brief.how_it_works: Operations are chained together as a data flow graph to represent the desired pipeline. The homepage does not go deeper into the internals than that.
brief.standout: GEGL works as a node graph of operations, and the same syntax used to build flows interactively in GIMP also works on the command line. It also supports floating point, non-destructive processing, and it underpins GIMP itself.
brief.status: Probably maintained, but only weakly evidenced. The homepage says 'Last updated 2025-04-18 18:03:50 CEST'. The GNOME GitLab project page shows it was created May 22, 2018, but it showed no recent commit or release date. The README was not visible through that page.
brief.caveats: I saw no real command lines, so the brief has no usage examples. The GitLab page returned only metadata (GNU GPLv3, created date) and no README text. The homepage does not say what gegl and gegl-imgcmp do individually, so I did not describe them. Installation details beyond the brew package are unknown.

entry.title: GEGL
entry.tldr: The node-graph image engine under GIMP, with a command-line tool for chaining pixel operations into pipelines in floating point.
entry.deeper_look:
GEGL, the Generic Graphics Library, is a data flow image processing framework. Instead of applying one edit after another to a bitmap, you describe a pipeline: load an image, adjust colour, apply a filter, store the result. The operations are chained into a graph, and the graph is the description of the work.

The homepage says it provides "floating point processing and non-destructive image processing capabilities". Floating point means intermediate results are not squeezed into 8 bits at each step. Non-destructive means the original is untouched and the graph can be changed and re-run. GEGL supplies the operations for loading and storing images, colour adjustments, and GIMP's artistic filters.

It was built as the engine for GIMP, and other projects use it too, including imgflo, GNOME Photos and iconographer. The brief says the command-line syntax matches the one used to build processing flows interactively in GIMP. That makes the terminal a plain way to see what a graph of image operations looks like without a GUI around it.

The brew formula installs two executables, gegl and gegl-imgcmp. The homepage does not say exactly what each does, so start with the help output.

Prints the usage text for the second installed tool, so you can see what it does.

entry.whats_unique: It is the actual graph-based engine behind GIMP, usable outside the GUI with the same syntax for describing pipelines. Most image command-line tools apply one edit at a time; this one treats the pipeline as the thing you build.
entry.caveats: The brief found no usage examples and no README, so expect to learn from --help and the project site. Maintenance looks likely but is only weakly evidenced.
